why: C (P, T, U, R) ranks by the worst year alone, A and D are the two ranking fillers the source also has, and ranking by peak growth landing on B is the slip the source names; reading the credit-risk or customs row instead ties P and T, so it points equally at B and C, and a stricter reading would count that as a wrong-row slip landing on the answer.

A holds if a candidate reads the private hire row in place of arcade (294 of 402 is 73%), B looks true if tickets (+24, 16%) are read in place of private hire against food and drink, and D comes from comparing margins instead of revenue-weighted profits; the percentage-point slip leads away from C.

Options form a tight $10 grid (about 5% of $183) on a maximum-price question, so neighbours are rough-estimate landings, and the one slip that lands on $183 (pricing each visit at the hourly rate, ignoring time per visit) is the slip the source names.

€1,971 applies the 6.6-point margin difference (or the Nov-Dec margin) to January revenue, €1,777 applies that margin difference to Nov-Dec costs, and €1,618 is the numeric filler the source allows, continuing the roughly 10% ratio spacing (1,777 ÷ 1,618 = 1.10); leaving out the cost rise gives €1,874, which lands on no option.

B forgets to adjust for sailing days (total passengers fall about 5%), C reverses the sign, D reverses the sign and skips the per-day step, and the wrong-base slip that still gives 3% is the one the source names.

A reverses the comparison (agency hours added 33 points against an 11-point rise in calls), B over-reads both index lines sitting at 100 in Week -3, and D compares point changes (-75 against -100) instead of proportions; reading agency hours as a level instead of a share also lands on C, which only roughly matches the source's named slip of reading the staff line instead of total hours.
The options are all four countries on offer, and the column slips lead to wrong options (packs alone, cost or price give D; pack size alone gives B), so none lands on C.

A holds for the wrong row (farming's 7% beats film and media's 2%), and C extends the forecast trend, which comes true if a candidate projects a decade too far; D (under 10%) needs a candidate to divide 72 by the forecast-year total (768, giving 9.4%) or to mistake farming's 7% growth for its share, a weaker slip that a stricter reading might reject.

A is a near miss (3.5 times read as 3, or industry profits read half a gridline low), C's 7% is the industry-profits line read in place of Pestora's profits, and D compares revenue only, ignoring the margin dip; no common slip gives a 4% fall (revenue alone or margin alone give 2%).

A's 27% leaves breakfast (or banqueting) out of food and drink, C's 23% wrongly counts banqueting as an other service (33 of 141), and D is a near-miss threshold (3.6% against 4%); no slip keeps B true without also making a wrong statement true.
